 Study Identifies Twenty-Eight Sub-Municipal Dengue Clusters Across Colombia’s Valle del Cauca

 Study Identifies Twenty-Eight Sub-Municipal Dengue Clusters Across Colombia's Valle del Cauca
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 Researchers examining the transmission of dengue virus in Colombia’s department of Valle del Cauca identified twenty-eight localized disease clusters occurring at the sub-municipal level throughout 2022. The retrospective observational study evaluated laboratory-confirmed cases to map the precise geographic and temporal dimensions of infection, providing critical spatial resolution for public health agencies aiming to deploy reactive vector control measures. By analyzing geographic coordinates linked to patient residences alongside official consultation dates, the investigative team demonstrated that local transmission events routinely concentrate within tightly defined neighborhood boundaries while persisting across shifting climatic periods.
 Dengue remains an endemic public health concern throughout Valle del Cauca, yet the exact spatial scale and temporal timing of seasonal transmission necessary to execute effective reactive interventions have historically remained unclear across the department’s forty-two municipalities. To resolve this operational gap, the authors established two primary research aims. The first focused on identifying statistically significant spatio-temporal dengue clusters within defined municipal zones. The secondary aim evaluated the relationship between patients’ demographic and clinical characteristics and their likelihood of requiring hospitalization for dengue care.
 The investigation drew data directly from the Sistema Nacional de Vigilancia en Salud Pública, Colombia’s national public health surveillance network known as SIVIGILA. Healthcare providers across Valle del Cauca reported a total of 3,964 dengue cases during the 2022 calendar year, of which 2,232 cases—or 56 percent—were confirmed through laboratory diagnostics. For the purpose of spatial analysis, the investigators utilized each patient’s documented residential geolocation as the probable site of viral infection. Among the laboratory-confirmed records, 1,973 cases fell within the specified spatial boundaries of nine municipalities selected for detailed clustering assessment, which was executed using Kulldorff’s space-time scan statistic and mapped using the R programming environment.
 The space-time scan statistic uncovered twenty-eight distinct clusters at the sub-municipal level, encompassing radii between 0 and 0.98 kilometers. These transmission foci endured for durations spanning one to six months and contained case counts ranging from 10 to 114 individuals. In total, the identified clusters accounted for 32.0 percent of the 1,973 cases analyzed within the nine municipalities. Notably, twenty-six of the twenty-eight clusters—representing 92.9 percent—spanned both warm-dry and cool-wet seasonal phases, demonstrating that localized viral activity regularly bridged contrasting meteorological periods rather than confining itself exclusively to a single seasonal window.
 Beyond mapping spatial boundaries, the research team analyzed factors driving severe disease manifestations, noting that 960 patients within the overall cohort were hospitalized. Multivariable evaluations revealed substantial disparities across socioeconomic brackets and age groups. Patients classified within a lower socioeconomic status faced an estimated 30 percent increase in the odds of hospitalization compared to individuals of higher economic standing, with an odds ratio of 1.30 and a 95 percent confidence interval between 1.07 and 1.57. Furthermore, individuals enrolled in Colombia’s state-subsidized health insurance scheme exhibited significantly elevated odds of hospital admission compared to those participating in the contributory insurance system, reflected by an odds ratio of 1.74 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.41 to 2.15.
 Age also represented a key determinant of clinical escalation, as individuals aged 70 years or older experienced more than double the odds of hospital admission compared to younger adults between the ages of 20 and 29 years, yielding an odds ratio of 2.47 and a 95 percent confidence interval from 1.51 to 4.04. The authors concluded that pinpointing sub-municipal dengue clusters reveals highly actionable spatial targets capable of guiding reactive local mosquito control programs, while underscoring that dengue places an unequal burden on socioeconomically vulnerable communities and older populations in Valle del Cauca.
 Subject of Research: Spatio-temporal clustering and hospitalization risk factors of dengue in Valle del Cauca, Colombia
 Article Title: Spatio-temporal clustering of dengue in Valle del Cauca, Colombia
